body:
The development of Puranic Hindu traditions

Hindu religious traditions developed through interaction among Vedic teachings, philosophical systems, regional forms of worship, devotional movements and temple institutions.

During the early centuries of the Common Era, worship centred on particular deities became increasingly important. The Puranas helped integrate regional deities, legends, pilgrimage traditions and religious practices into wider religious frameworks.

The Puranas contain narratives relating to creation, divine manifestations, genealogies, religious duties, pilgrimage and sacred places. Many were intended for public recitation, allowing religious narratives to circulate among people who did not have access to formal Vedic education.

Principal traditions of worship

TraditionPrincipal deity or conceptGujarat example
VaishnavismVishnu and his manifestationsDwarkadhish Temple, Dwarka
ShaivismShivaSomnath Temple
ShaktismDevi or divine feminine powerAmbaji and Kalika Mata, Pavagadh
Saura traditionSurya, the Sun deitySun Temple, Modhera

Vaishnavism recognises divine incarnations or Avatars, particularly the manifestations of Vishnu. Rama and Krishna became central to major devotional and literary traditions.

Shaiva traditions include worship of Shiva in anthropomorphic forms and through the Linga. Shakta traditions give central importance to the divine feminine, understood as Shakti or cosmic power.

These traditions are not necessarily mutually exclusive. Individuals and communities may honour multiple deities while maintaining particular devotional affiliations.

The Bhagavad Gita

The Bhagavad Gita forms part of the Bhishma Parva of the Mahabharata. It presents a dialogue between Krishna and Arjuna concerning duty, moral uncertainty, knowledge and spiritual liberation.

The text brings together several approaches to spiritual life:

  • Karma Yoga: Performing one's duties without selfish attachment to the results of action.
  • Jnana Yoga: Pursuing spiritual knowledge and understanding the nature of reality.
  • Bhakti Yoga: Devotion and surrender to the divine.

The Gita does not simply recommend abandoning all action. An important teaching is that responsible action can become a spiritual discipline when undertaken without selfish attachment.

Nishkama Karma

Action performed without selfish desire for its fruits or rewards. The emphasis is on fulfilling duty without becoming attached to personal gain.

Vedanta and its principal texts

Vedanta investigates the nature of Brahman, the individual self and the relationship between ultimate reality and the experienced world.

Its 3 principal textual foundations are collectively known as the Prasthanatrayi: the Upanishads, the Bhagavad Gita and the Brahma Sutra.

Different Vedantic thinkers interpreted these shared texts differently, giving rise to several philosophical schools.

Major schools of Vedanta

Advaita of Adi Shankaracharya

Adi Shankaracharya, generally associated with the 8th century CE, developed the influential school of Advaita, or non-dualism.

Advaita holds that Brahman alone is ultimately real and that the deepest nature of Atman is not different from Brahman. Ignorance causes individuals to experience themselves as separate and limited beings. Spiritual knowledge removes this ignorance.

The concept of Maya helps explain the experienced world and apparent multiplicity. Advaita does not mean that ordinary experience has no practical existence; it distinguishes empirical experience from ultimate reality.

Tradition associates Shankaracharya with 4 major monastic centres: Sringeri in Karnataka, Puri in Odisha, Jyotirmath near Badrinath in Uttarakhand and Sharada Math at Dwarka in Gujarat.

Vishishtadvaita of Ramanujacharya

Ramanuja, associated with the 11th and 12th centuries, developed Vishishtadvaita, or qualified non-dualism.

He regarded Brahman, identified with the personal Supreme Being, as the unity within which individual souls and the material world have real existence. Souls remain distinguishable rather than losing their individuality completely.

Ramanuja emphasised devotion, surrender and divine grace. His teachings became fundamental to the Sri Vaishnava tradition.

Dvaita of Madhvacharya

Madhvacharya, associated with the 13th century, taught Dvaita, or dualism. He maintained a real distinction between God and individual souls. Vishnu is the independent Supreme Being, while souls depend upon him.

His teaching places strong emphasis on devotion and divine grace. Udupi in Karnataka became an important centre of his tradition.

Dvaitadvaita and Shuddhadvaita

Nimbarkacharya is associated with Dvaitadvaita, the doctrine that individual souls and the world are both different and non-different from Brahman and depend upon it.

Vallabhacharya developed Shuddhadvaita, or pure non-dualism. In his philosophy, Krishna is the supreme Brahman, and the world is a real manifestation of the divine rather than merely an illusion. His devotional path, Pushtimarg, became particularly influential in Gujarat and Rajasthan.

Prelims focus

  • The Bhagavad Gita forms part of the Mahabharata.
  • Prasthanatrayi consists of the Upanishads, Bhagavad Gita and Brahma Sutra.
  • Shankaracharya taught Advaita; Ramanuja taught Vishishtadvaita.
  • Madhvacharya taught Dvaita; Nimbarka taught Dvaitadvaita.
  • Vallabhacharya taught Shuddhadvaita and established Pushtimarg.
  • Trap: Vedanta is a broad philosophical tradition; it is not synonymous only with Shankaracharya's Advaita.

[References: NCERT, Class 12, Themes in Indian History Part I, Theme 4, Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings, pp. 104–107; NCERT, Class 7, Our Pasts II, 2020–21, Chapter 8, Devotional Paths to the Divine, pp. 104–107; NCERT, Class 11, Knowledge Traditions and Practices of India, Chapter 2, Indian Philosophical Systems; IGNOU, Eastern Philosophy, Block 1, section on Shuddhadvaita; University of Calicut, The Systems of Indian Philosophy; online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: The principal interpretations within Vedanta.

title: Puranic Hindu Traditions, the Bhagavad Gita and Vedanta

body:
Meaning and development of Bhakti

Bhakti means loving devotion to the divine. It can involve prayer, remembrance, singing, surrender, worship and service. Devotional traditions developed in ancient India and acquired increasingly important regional forms during the medieval period.

The Bhakti movement was not a single centrally organised movement. It included different traditions, communities, philosophical schools and saint-poets who flourished in different regions and periods.

Many Bhakti teachers argued that sincere devotion was more important than social status, expensive rituals or mastery of scholarly languages. Some openly challenged caste discrimination and religious hypocrisy, while others worked within established temple and religious institutions.

Saguna and Nirguna Bhakti

Saguna Bhakti is devotion to the divine understood as possessing attributes or a particular form. Devotion to Krishna, Rama and Shiva are important examples.

Nirguna Bhakti emphasises the divine beyond physical form and limiting attributes. Nirguna saints frequently criticised the assumption that God could be reached only through external images, ritual or institutional authority.

The distinction concerns the way the divine is understood and approached. Saguna and Nirguna traditions share an emphasis on devotion, but they differ in their interpretation of divine form.

The Tamil Bhakti tradition

From approximately the 6th to 9th centuries CE, the Alvars and Nayanars developed influential devotional traditions in the Tamil region. They travelled to sacred places and composed hymns in Tamil, connecting religious devotion with local language, music and pilgrimage.

FeatureAlvarsNayanars
Devotional traditionVaishnavismShaivism
Traditional number1263
Important saintsAndal, Nammalvar, PeriyalvarAppar, Sambandar, Sundarar, Karaikkal Ammaiyar
Important literatureNalayira Divya PrabandhamTevaram and the broader Shaiva hymn tradition

The Nalayira Divya Prabandham, an anthology of approximately 4000 sacred compositions, became especially important in Tamil Vaishnavism. It is sometimes described as the Tamil Veda.

The Tevaram contains hymns of Appar, Sambandar and Sundarar. Manikkavasagar, another important Tamil Shaiva poet, is associated with the Tiruvacakam.

Andal was a woman Alvar devoted to Vishnu. Karaikkal Ammaiyar was a woman saint of the Shaiva tradition. Their compositions illustrate the contribution of women to devotional literature.

Temple patronage and art

Chola and Pandya rulers supported temples associated with devotional saints. Their patronage connected religious worship with monumental architecture, sculpture, music and public festivals.

The Chola period produced celebrated bronze representations of Shiva, including Nataraja. Tamil Shaiva hymns became part of temple worship, demonstrating the relationship between devotional poetry and religious institutions.

Basavanna and Virashaivism

During the 12th century, Basavanna became a leading figure of the Virashaiva or Lingayat movement in Karnataka. Other prominent figures included Allama Prabhu and Akkamahadevi.

The movement challenged hereditary social hierarchy and many conventional religious practices. It emphasised personal devotion to Shiva, ethical conduct and the dignity of work.

Its teachings were expressed through short Kannada compositions called Vachanas. Many Vachanas criticised social inequality and religious hypocrisy in accessible language.

The personal Ishtalinga became an important religious symbol within the tradition. Criticism of conventional temple rituals therefore did not mean rejection of every religious symbol.

The Varkari tradition of Maharashtra

The Varkari devotional tradition centres on Vitthala or Vithoba, a form of Vishnu or Krishna, whose major shrine is at Pandharpur in Maharashtra.

Varkari saints emphasised devotion, remembrance, pilgrimage and moral life. Many rejected the belief that renunciation of family and occupation was necessary for spiritual progress.

SaintPrincipal literary or devotional association
JnaneshwarJnaneshwari, a Marathi exposition of the Bhagavad Gita
NamdevVitthala devotion and devotional poetry
EknathMarathi religious literature and devotion
TukaramAbhangas expressing devotion and ethical concerns
ChokhamelaDevotional poetry challenging caste exclusion

The Abhanga is an important Marathi devotional poetic form. The pilgrimage to Pandharpur continues to express the communal character of the Varkari tradition.

Prelims focus

  • The 12 Alvars were Vaishnava saints; the 63 Nayanars were Shaiva saints.
  • Nalayira Divya Prabandham belongs to the Alvar tradition.
  • Tevaram is associated with Appar, Sambandar and Sundarar.
  • Basavanna, Allama Prabhu and Akkamahadevi belong to the Virashaiva tradition.
  • Varkari devotion centres on Vitthala at Pandharpur.
  • Trap: Bhakti did not uniformly reject temple worship, images or all established religious institutions.

[References: NCERT, Class 7, Our Pasts II, 2020–21, Chapter 8, Devotional Paths to the Divine, pp. 104–110; NCERT, Class 12, Themes in Indian History Part II, Theme 6, Bhakti-Sufi Traditions, pp. 142–148; Gujarat State School Textbook Board, Class 7, Social Science, 2021–22, Chapter 7, Bhakti Age: Religious Sects and Saints, online textbook copy consulted 26 November 2026; the corresponding project scan was unreadable.]

pictures.alt: Saguna understands the divine through attributes or forms; Nirguna goes beyond physical form and limiting attributes. Both emphasise devotion.
pictures.caption: Two broad approaches to Bhakti.

title: The Bhakti Tradition: Southern and Regional Devotional Movements

body:
The spread of vernacular devotional traditions

From the medieval period onwards, Bhakti traditions expanded across northern, western and eastern India. Saint-poets composed in languages understood by ordinary people, allowing devotional ideas to circulate through singing, oral narration and community gatherings.

These traditions influenced the development of Hindi, Bengali, Assamese, Marathi, Gujarati and other regional literary languages.

Important Bhakti saints of northern India

Ramananda

Ramananda is traditionally associated with Rama devotion and the growth of the Rama-centred Bhakti tradition in northern India. His religious lineage is associated with greater accessibility of devotion to people from diverse social backgrounds.

Kabir

Kabir, associated with the 15th century, was an influential Nirguna saint traditionally connected with the weaving community of Banaras.

He emphasised direct spiritual experience, devotion to the formless divine and ethical conduct. He criticised caste discrimination, religious hypocrisy and mechanical adherence to outward Hindu and Muslim rituals.

His compositions include Dohas, Sakhis and Pads. Verses attributed to him have been preserved in the Bijak, the Guru Granth Sahib and other collections.

Ravidas

Ravidas was a prominent devotional saint associated with a community historically subjected to caste discrimination. His teachings emphasised spiritual equality, devotion and human dignity.

His concept of Begampura expresses the ideal of a society free from suffering and oppressive social distinctions. Some of his compositions are included in the Guru Granth Sahib.

Tulsidas

Tulsidas was a major poet of Saguna Rama Bhakti. His best-known work, the Ramcharitmanas, presents the story of Rama in Awadhi. The Vinaya Patrika is another important devotional work associated with him.

His writings contributed significantly to the spread of Rama devotion through a widely understood regional language.

Surdas

Surdas is associated with Krishna devotion, particularly narratives of Krishna's childhood and divine play. His compositions are preserved in collections such as the Sursagar.

Braj Bhasha became an important literary language through this devotional tradition. Surdas is traditionally associated with the Pushtimarg literary tradition.

Mirabai

Mirabai was a 16th-century Krishna devotee associated with Rajasthan and Gujarat. Her songs express intense personal devotion to Krishna, often addressed as Giridhar Gopal.

Her devotional life and poetry challenged many expectations placed upon women within aristocratic and patriarchal social structures. Her compositions remain part of the living musical heritage of western India.

Bhakti in eastern India

FigureRegionPrincipal contribution
JayadevaEastern IndiaGita Govinda, a Sanskrit devotional poem on Krishna and Radha
Chaitanya MahaprabhuBengal and OdishaKrishna devotion and congregational Sankirtana
Srimanta SankaradevaAssamEka Sarana Nama Dharma, devotional literature and religious institutions

Chaitanya emphasised loving devotion to Krishna and collective singing of the divine name, known as Sankirtana.

Sankaradeva promoted devotion to a single Supreme Being, worshipped through the Vaishnava tradition. He established or inspired Satras, which became religious and cultural institutions, and Namghars, which serve as community prayer and devotional gathering places. The Kirtana-ghosha is an important work associated with him.

Sikhism and Guru Nanak

Sikhism emerged as a distinct religious tradition in Punjab through the teachings of Guru Nanak and the succeeding Sikh Gurus.

Guru Nanak emphasised belief in one divine reality, remembrance of the divine name, honest work, sharing with others and equality. He criticised caste distinctions, religious hypocrisy and empty ritualism.

His teachings encouraged spiritual life while participating responsibly in society rather than requiring withdrawal from household life.

Important principles are commonly expressed through the following terms:

  • Naam Japna: Remembering and meditating upon the divine name.
  • Kirat Karni: Earning one's livelihood honestly.
  • Vand Chhakna: Sharing one's resources with others.

Major developments under the Sikh Gurus

GuruPrincipal contribution
Guru NanakFounder of Sikhism
Guru AngadStandardisation and promotion of the Gurmukhi script
Guru Ram DasDevelopment of the settlement that became Amritsar
Guru ArjanCompilation of the Adi Granth in 1604
Guru Gobind SinghEstablishment of the Khalsa in 1699 and recognition of scripture as the enduring Guru

The Guru Granth Sahib is the central scripture and enduring spiritual Guru of Sikhism. It contains compositions of Sikh Gurus as well as those of other religious figures, including Kabir, Namdev, Ravidas and Sheikh Farid.

The Gurdwara is a Sikh place of worship. The Langar, or community kitchen, expresses the principles of service and equality through shared meals irrespective of social background.

Sikhism shares certain historical and intellectual concerns with Bhakti and Sufi traditions, but it possesses its own scriptures, institutions, religious identity and historical development.

Prelims focus

  • Kabir is associated with Nirguna Bhakti and the Bijak.
  • Tulsidas composed the Ramcharitmanas in Awadhi.
  • Surdas is associated with Krishna devotion and the Sursagar.
  • Chaitanya promoted Sankirtana; Sankaradeva is associated with Satras and Namghars.
  • Guru Arjan compiled the Adi Granth in 1604; Guru Gobind Singh established the Khalsa in 1699.
  • Trap: Guru Nanak founded Sikhism, whereas Guru Gobind Singh founded the Khalsa.

[References: NCERT, Class 7, Our Pasts II, 2020–21, Chapter 8, Devotional Paths to the Divine, pp. 113–120; NCERT, Class 12, Themes in Indian History Part II, Theme 6, Bhakti-Sufi Traditions, sections on Kabir, Guru Nanak and Mirabai; Gujarat State School Textbook Board, Class 7, Social Science, 2021–22, Chapter 7, Bhakti Age: Religious Sects and Saints, online copy consulted 26 November 2026.]
